questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Calculate the Price Elasticity of demand when the price increases from 100 FCFA to 175 FCFA.

(4 marks)

(ii) Calculate the Price Elasticity of Supply when the price falls from 200 FCFA to 175 FCFA.

(4 marks)

(iii) Briefly explain Two (02) importance of price elasticity of demand to the government.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Price elasticity of demand (PED), price rising from 100 FCFA to 175 FCFA.**

From the table, the quantity demanded falls from 60 kg (at 100 FCFA) to 25 kg (at 175 FCFA).

$$
\text{PED}=\frac{\%\ \text{change in quantity demanded}}{\%\ \text{change in price}}
$$

- Change in quantity demanded: $25-60=-35$ kg, so $\%\Delta Q_d=\dfrac{-35}{60}\times100=-58.33\%$.
- Change in price: $175-100=75$ FCFA, so $\%\Delta P=\dfrac{75}{100}\times100=75\%$.

$$
\text{PED}=\frac{-58.33}{75}=-0.78
$$

PED is about $-0.78$ (an absolute value of **0.78**). Since $0.78<1$, demand for apples is **price inelastic** over this range: the quantity demanded falls by less than the percentage rise in price. (The minus sign only shows that price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.)

*Note.* Here the percentage changes are measured from the starting values, the usual O Level method. The mid-point (arc) formula would give about $-1.51$.

**(ii) Price elasticity of supply (PES), price falling from 200 FCFA to 175 FCFA.**

From the table, the quantity supplied falls from 175 kg (at 200 FCFA) to 150 kg (at 175 FCFA).

$$
\text{PES}=\frac{\%\ \text{change in quantity supplied}}{\%\ \text{change in price}}
$$

- $\%\Delta Q_s=\dfrac{150-175}{175}\times100=\dfrac{-25}{175}\times100=-14.29\%$.
- $\%\Delta P=\dfrac{175-200}{200}\times100=\dfrac{-25}{200}\times100=-12.5\%$.

$$
\text{PES}=\frac{-14.29}{-12.5}=+1.14
$$

PES is about **1.14**. Since $1.14>1$, supply is **price elastic** over this range: the quantity supplied falls by a larger percentage than the price. (Here both changes are negative, so the answer is positive.)

**(iii) Two importance of price elasticity of demand to the government.**

1. **Choosing goods to tax and forecasting tax revenue.** If the government taxes a good whose demand is *inelastic* (for example fuel, salt or tobacco), the quantity bought falls only slightly, so tax revenue rises. If it taxed a good with *elastic* demand, consumers would cut their purchases sharply and revenue would fall. Knowing the PED helps the government to decide which goods to tax and how much revenue to expect.
2. **Deciding price and subsidy policies.** If demand for a basic good such as bread or rice is inelastic, a price rise hurts consumers a great deal, so the government may fix a maximum price or give a subsidy to protect them. Equally, to discourage the consumption of harmful goods the government must know that a tax will cut demand strongly only when demand is elastic.

*Other acceptable points:* effects of devaluation on export and import earnings, and pricing of public services.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given Qd = 30 - 2P and Qs = 2P - 10:

Determine;

i) the equilibrium quantity.

(4 marks)

ii) the equilibrium price.

(4 marks)

**Note:** Qd = Quantity demanded; Qs = Quantity supply; P = Price
questions.corrige_markdown:
At equilibrium the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied: $Q_d=Q_s$. We find the price first, because the quantity is then read from either equation.

**ii) Equilibrium price.**

$$
30-2P=2P-10
$$

$$
30+10=2P+2P
$$

$$
40=4P
$$

$$
P=\frac{40}{4}=10
$$

The equilibrium price is **$P=10$** (in the price units of the question).

**i) Equilibrium quantity.** Substitute $P=10$ in the demand equation:

$$
Q_d=30-2(10)=30-20=10
$$

Check with the supply equation: $Q_s=2(10)-10=20-10=10$. Both equations give the same quantity, so the equilibrium quantity is **$Q=10$ units**.

**Answer:** equilibrium price $=10$ and equilibrium quantity $=10$ units.
